title: Star Trails over Rubin
caption: Star trails above Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Cerro Pachón
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site
credit: NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA/P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Stars sweep across the southern sky above the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory, perched on Cerro Pachón, in this long exposure. That motion is only apparent, produced as Earth rotates. Rubin itself is built to capture real change in the Universe on a far larger scale.

When this photograph was released, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) was still ahead. Over its 10 years, Rubin's data processing was expected to produce around 500 petabytes, more than all the text humans have ever written, in every language. The plan was for Rubin to scan the sky nightly with its LSST Camera.

By returning to the same sky again and again, Rubin was expected to flag millions of changes across the south every night, among them supernovae and pulsating variable stars. Its software compares each new image with earlier ones and picks out differences in near-real time. That gives scientists a better chance of finding and studying rare, short-lived events throughout the Universe.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by Petr Horálek. No camera or exposure details or colour mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.
